name: Learn: Pod Design
objective: CKAD › Application Design & Build (20%). Goal: compose multi-container Pods — sidecars sharing an emptyDir, init containers that prepare volumes, liveness/readiness/startup probes, and lifecycle hooks with a termination grace period — the Pod-design building blocks the exam expects you to write by hand.
description: Master Pod design step by step — sidecar containers sharing a volume, init containers, liveness/readiness/startup probes, and postStart/preStop lifecycle hooks with terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Build each pattern with plain kubectl and YAML.

questions.title: Sidecar sharing an emptyDir volume
questions.teach:
A **Pod** can run more than one container. A common pattern is a **sidecar**: a helper container that runs alongside the main app and cooperates through a **shared volume**.

The simplest shared volume is an **emptyDir** — an empty directory created when the Pod starts and mounted into every container that asks for it. Containers mount the *same* emptyDir at (possibly different) paths, so whatever one writes the other can read.

Here the main `nginx` container serves files from `/usr/share/nginx/html`, while a busybox **sidecar** writes content into that same directory — the sidecar produces, nginx serves.

**Ways to share data between containers:**
- **emptyDir** — scratch space tied to the Pod's lifetime; deleted when the Pod is removed. `emptyDir: {}` is disk-backed; `emptyDir: {medium: Memory}` is a tmpfs (RAM); `sizeLimit` caps it.
- **configMap / secret volume** — inject config as files.
- **PVC** — durable storage that survives the Pod.
- **downwardAPI / projected** — expose Pod metadata or combine several sources.

**Classic sidecar vs native sidecar:** a *plain* sidecar is just a second entry under `containers` (what this step builds). A **native sidecar** (1.29+) is an `initContainer` with `restartPolicy: Always` — it starts before the app, stays running, and is terminated after the app, which fixes ordering/shutdown problems the plain pattern has.

**Gotchas:**
- Both containers must declare a `volumeMounts` entry whose `name` matches the `volumes` entry — a volume defined but not mounted does nothing.
- `mountPath` can differ per container; the `name` is what links them.
- All Pod containers share the network namespace (`localhost`, port space) but **not** the filesystem — only mounted volumes are shared.
- A sidecar that exits turns the Pod `NotReady`/`Error`; keep it alive (e.g. `sleep`) unless using the native-sidecar pattern.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `pod-design`, create a Pod `web-sidecar` with:
- container `web` using image `nginx:1.25`, mounting an emptyDir volume `content` at `/usr/share/nginx/html`
- a sidecar container `writer` using image `busybox:1.36` that mounts the **same** `content` volume at `/data` and runs `sh -c 'echo hello-from-sidecar > /data/index.html; sleep 3600'`

Target: `kubectl -n pod-design get pod web-sidecar` is Running with 2/2 ready, both containers share the `content` emptyDir, and `writer` mounts it at `/data`.
questions.hint: Write a Pod spec with two entries under `containers` and one `emptyDir` volume under `volumes`. Each container needs a matching `volumeMounts` entry referencing `name: content`. Apply with `kubectl apply -f`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-sidecar
  namespace: pod-design
spec:
  volumes:
  - name: content
    emptyDir: {}
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    volumeMounts:
    - name: content
      mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
  - name: writer
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","echo hello-from-sidecar > /data/index.html; sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: content
      mountPath: /data
YAML
kubectl -n pod-design get pod web-sidecar -w

verification.description: web-sidecar runs 2 containers sharing the 'content' emptyDir

questions.title: Init container preparing a shared volume
questions.teach:
An **init container** runs to completion *before* the app containers start. If there are several, they run one at a time, in order; the app containers only start once all init containers have exited successfully.

A classic use is **preparing a shared volume**: the init container writes a file (or clones a repo, or fetches config) into an emptyDir, then the main container — which mounts the same volume — finds the data already in place when it boots.

Unlike a sidecar, the init container is *gone* by the time the app runs; it only sets the stage.

**Common uses of init containers:**
- Prepare/seed a shared volume (this step).
- Wait for a dependency (poll a Service/DB until it responds) so the app starts only when ready.
- Run a migration or fetch a secret/artifact before the app boots.

**Init vs native sidecar:** a regular `initContainer` must **exit 0** before the next one (and the app) runs. An `initContainer` with `restartPolicy: Always` is a **native sidecar** (1.29+) — it *stays running* alongside the app instead of completing, which is how you model a long-lived helper that must be up before the main container.

**Gotchas:**
- Order matters: init containers run sequentially in the listed order; a failing init container is **retried** per the Pod's `restartPolicy` and blocks the whole Pod (`Init:Error`/`Init:CrashLoopBackOff`).
- Init containers can have their own `resources`, `securityContext`, and `volumeMounts`.
- Probes don't apply to ordinary init containers.
- `kubectl logs <pod> -c <initname>` to debug; `kubectl describe pod` shows init status.
- An init container finishing does **not** keep its files unless they were written to a shared volume (its own rootfs is gone when it exits).
questions.prompt:
In namespace `pod-design`, create a Pod `init-prep` with:
- an emptyDir volume `shared`
- an init container `setup` using `busybox:1.36` that runs `sh -c 'echo ready > /work/status.txt'`, mounting `shared` at `/work`
- a main container `app` using `busybox:1.36` that mounts `shared` at `/work` and runs `sh -c 'cat /work/status.txt; sleep 3600'`

Target: `kubectl -n pod-design get pod init-prep` is Running (init completed), and the `setup` init container prepared `/work/status.txt` in the shared volume before `app` started.
questions.hint: Put the init container under `spec.initContainers` and the app under `spec.containers`; both reference the same volume `shared`. The main container prints the file the init container wrote.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: init-prep
  namespace: pod-design
spec:
  volumes:
  - name: shared
    emptyDir: {}
  initContainers:
  - name: setup
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","echo ready > /work/status.txt"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: shared
      mountPath: /work
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","cat /work/status.txt; sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: shared
      mountPath: /work
YAML
kubectl -n pod-design get pod init-prep -w

verification.description: init-prep has an init container that prepared the shared volume

questions.title: Liveness + readiness probes (httpGet)
questions.teach:
**Probes** let the kubelet check container health:
- A **liveness probe** answers “is this container still healthy?” — if it fails repeatedly, the kubelet **restarts** the container.
- A **readiness probe** answers “is this container ready to receive traffic?” — if it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints (but *not* restarted).
- A **startup probe** gates the other two for slow starters (see the next step).

An **httpGet** probe sends an HTTP request to a `path` on a `port`; any 2xx/3xx response is a pass. `initialDelaySeconds` delays the first check; `periodSeconds` sets the interval.

**Four handler types** (pick exactly one per probe):
- `httpGet` — `path` + `port` (+ optional `httpHeaders`, `scheme: HTTPS`).
- `exec` — runs a `command` in the container; exit 0 = pass.
- `tcpSocket` — opens a TCP connection to a `port`.
- `grpc` — `port` (+ optional `service`) for gRPC health checks.

**Tuning fields:** `initialDelaySeconds`, `periodSeconds`, `timeoutSeconds`, `successThreshold`, `failureThreshold`.

**Gotchas:**
- `successThreshold` **must be 1** for liveness and startup probes; readiness may be >1.
- Liveness failure = restart (can cause crash loops if misconfigured); readiness failure = drop from endpoints but keep running.
- No probe at all = container is treated as ready/alive as soon as it's started — fine for simple pods, risky for real services.
- `httpGet` 2xx/3xx = pass; 4xx/5xx = fail.
- Set `initialDelaySeconds` generously or use a startup probe, otherwise a slow boot triggers premature restarts.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `pod-design`, create a Pod `probed` with one container `web` (`nginx:1.25`, containerPort 80) that has **both**:
- a liveness probe: httpGet path `/` on port 80, `initialDelaySeconds: 5`, `periodSeconds: 10`
- a readiness probe: httpGet path `/` on port 80, `initialDelaySeconds: 3`, `periodSeconds: 5`

Target: `kubectl -n pod-design get pod probed` is Running and 1/1 ready, with both an httpGet livenessProbe and an httpGet readinessProbe on the `web` container.
questions.hint: Under the container add `livenessProbe:` and `readinessProbe:`, each with an `httpGet:` block (`path` and `port`). nginx serves `/` on port 80 so both probes pass.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: probed
  namespace: pod-design
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /
        port: 80
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /
        port: 80
      initialDelaySeconds: 3
      periodSeconds: 5
YAML
kubectl -n pod-design get pod probed -w

verification.description: probed has httpGet liveness AND readiness probes and is ready

questions.title: Startup probe + readiness probe
questions.teach:
A **startup probe** protects **slow-starting** containers. While it is running, the liveness and readiness probes are **disabled**, so a container that takes a while to boot isn't killed prematurely. Once the startup probe succeeds once, the other probes take over.

The key knob is `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` — that product is the maximum time the container is allowed to start. Pair it with a **readiness probe** so the Pod only receives traffic after it's both started *and* ready.

**Same handlers as any probe:** `httpGet`, `exec`, `tcpSocket`, or `grpc` — the startup probe isn't limited to HTTP.

**How the three probes relate:**
- Startup probe runs **first and alone**; liveness/readiness are held off until it passes once.
- After it passes, it never runs again; liveness and readiness take over.
- Use it instead of a huge `initialDelaySeconds` on liveness — it's the cleaner way to give a slow app a long grace window without weakening steady-state checks.

**Gotchas:**
- `successThreshold` must be **1** for a startup probe.
- Max startup budget = `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` (here 30 × 10 = 300s). If the app isn't up by then, the kubelet kills and restarts it.
- A startup probe is optional; without one, liveness starts checking after its own `initialDelaySeconds`.
- Readiness still governs endpoint membership after startup succeeds, so a started-but-not-ready Pod gets no Service traffic.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `pod-design`, create a Pod `slow-start` with one container `web` (`nginx:1.25`, containerPort 80) that has:
- a **startup probe**: httpGet path `/` on port 80, `failureThreshold: 30`, `periodSeconds: 10`
- a **readiness probe**: httpGet path `/` on port 80, `periodSeconds: 5`

Target: `kubectl -n pod-design get pod slow-start` is Running and 1/1 ready, with both an httpGet startupProbe and an httpGet readinessProbe on the `web` container.
questions.hint: Add `startupProbe:` and `readinessProbe:` under the container, each with an `httpGet:` block. The startup probe allows up to failureThreshold×periodSeconds (300s) for the container to come up.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: slow-start
  namespace: pod-design
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
    startupProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /
        port: 80
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /
        port: 80
      periodSeconds: 5
YAML
kubectl -n pod-design get pod slow-start -w

verification.description: slow-start has httpGet startup AND readiness probes and is ready

questions.title: Lifecycle hooks + terminationGracePeriodSeconds
questions.teach:
Containers can run **lifecycle hooks**:
- **postStart** fires right after the container is created — good for a one-time setup action.
- **preStop** fires right before the container is stopped (e.g. drain connections, flush state). It runs *before* the TERM signal is sent to the entrypoint.

`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` on the Pod is how long Kubernetes waits after starting shutdown (preStop + TERM) before force-killing with KILL. A well-behaved app uses preStop to finish in-flight work, sized to fit inside the grace period.

**Hook handler types:** both hooks accept `exec` (run a command), `httpGet`, or `tcpSocket` — same shape as probes, but no retries/thresholds.

**Shutdown sequence:** Pod marked Terminating → removed from endpoints → **preStop** runs → **SIGTERM** sent to PID 1 → wait up to `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` → **SIGKILL** if still alive.

**Gotchas:**
- The grace-period clock covers **preStop + SIGTERM together**. A `preStop` that sleeps 25s inside a 30s grace period leaves only ~5s for the app to handle TERM.
- **postStart has no ordering guarantee** relative to the container entrypoint — it may run before or after the main process starts, so don't depend on the app being up.
- A hook that fails (non-zero exit / bad HTTP) can kill the container (postStart) — keep hook commands simple and reliable.
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` defaults to **30**; set `0` only via force-delete. `kubectl delete --grace-period=` can override at delete time.
- Hooks run **at least once** but delivery isn't guaranteed if the node dies.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `pod-design`, create a Pod `graceful` with `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30` and one container `web` (`nginx:1.25`) that has a **lifecycle** block:
- a **postStart** exec hook running `sh -c 'echo started > /tmp/poststart'`
- a **preStop** exec hook running `sh -c 'sleep 5'`

Target: `kubectl -n pod-design get pod graceful` is Running, has `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`, and the `web` container has both a postStart and a preStop exec lifecycle hook.
questions.hint: Add `spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30` and a `lifecycle:` block under the container with `postStart.exec.command` and `preStop.exec.command`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: graceful
  namespace: pod-design
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    lifecycle:
      postStart:
        exec:
          command: ["sh","-c","echo started > /tmp/poststart"]
      preStop:
        exec:
          command: ["sh","-c","sleep 5"]
YAML
kubectl -n pod-design get pod graceful -w

verification.description: graceful has postStart+preStop hooks and grace period 30
